findings.description: Principle 4 (Mutual inhibition) Source column cites Guilford (1967) and Nijstad et al. (2010) — creativity and social psychology references — in a section introduced as '17 CPG principles from the neuroscience literature.' All other principles in these tables cite neuroscience sources (Graham Brown, von Holst, Grillner, Marder, Forssberg, etc.). The actual CPG concept of reciprocal inhibition between antagonist muscle groups originates from Graham Brown (1911) and Sherrington (1906). The Guilford/Nijstad references describe the AI analog (generative/evaluative processing competition) rather than the neuroscience origin. This creates attribution ambiguity: a reader following the Source column expects neuroscience citations and encounters creativity research instead.
findings.suggestion: Split the attribution: cite the CPG neuroscience source in the Source column (Graham Brown, 1911, or Sherrington, 1906, for reciprocal inhibition) and move the creativity references (Guilford, 1967; Nijstad et al., 2010) into the 'What the Gap Means' description, where they describe the AI-side analog. Alternatively, add a parenthetical note: 'Source (CPG origin): Graham Brown (1911); AI analog: Guilford (1967); Nijstad et al. (2010).'
